opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a very interesting relationship, and it's changed a lot in the past few years.

Traditionally, robotics was a field built on a very solid foundation: control theory, kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, state estimation. Robotics scholars spent decades making robots reliable, safe and precise, and that knowledge is extremely valuable. If you've ever tried to put a learned policy on a real arm or a humanoid, you quickly realize how much of that classical understanding you still need. Low-level control, hardware design, system integration: these are not things you can just learn away with a big neural network.

But embodied AI comes from a somewhat different starting point. Many of us came from computer vision, graphics, machine learning, and our question was: how do we make robots generalize? How do they handle open-ended environments, new objects, new instructions, the way large models handle language? Classical robotics often focused on a specific task done very well. Embodied AI cares about breadth, intelligence and generalization, and it relies heavily on data, simulation and learning.

So at first there was some tension. Some robotics people felt the AI side was too naive about the physical world, chasing demos that don't really work robustly. And some AI people felt traditional robotics was too hand-engineered, unable to scale. Honestly, both criticisms had some truth.

Now I see them converging. The field needs both. Large models give us semantic understanding, reasoning and task-level generalization. But to get reliable, dexterous action in the real world, you need robotics knowledge, good hardware, good control, and a deep respect for physics. In my own work, for example with simulation and synthetic data for training grasping and manipulation, the hardest problems are often exactly where learning meets physics.

So I don't see robotics scholars as being replaced by embodied AI, or embodied AI as just a rebranding of robotics. I see embodied AI as the next stage of robotics, where intelligence becomes the core question. The people who will make the biggest contributions are those who can bridge both worlds: who understand learning and data at scale, and also understand what it really takes to make a machine move in the physical world.

r002.rationale: It does not mention China or say that separation between robotics scholars and embodied AI persists there.

r003.rationale: The response says the fields are converging and that progress requires both, with contributors bridging robotics and embodied AI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the relationship is actually a bit complicated, and I say that as someone who came into this from the robotics side myself.

For a long time, robotics scholars were the people doing embodied intelligence before anyone called it that. The whole field was about perception, planning, control, grasping, locomotion. But the methodology was very different from what we now call embodied AI. It was model-based, it was physics-driven, it relied heavily on human-designed structure. You derived the dynamics, you built the controller, you tuned it on one specific platform.

Then the large-model wave came, and suddenly many of the most exciting results were coming from people with a vision or language or machine learning background, not from classical roboticists. That created some tension. Some robotics scholars felt that the new crowd didn't respect the hard problems, things like contact dynamics, safety, real-time constraints, hardware failure. And the new crowd sometimes felt that classical robotics was too conservative, too attached to hand-engineered pipelines that don't scale.

My own view is that both sides are half right, and the field is going to be built by people who can live in both worlds. Data-driven methods really do change what is possible, especially for generalization. You simply cannot hand-engineer your way to a robot that works in a thousand different kitchens. But data alone does not solve the physical world. The data is expensive, it is scarce compared to text and images, and the failure modes have consequences. The structure that roboticists understand, about kinematics, about geometry, about what makes a grasp stable, is exactly what you need to make learning sample-efficient and reliable.

So I see robotics scholars less as a group being displaced and more as a group being asked to change their role. Instead of designing the full solution by hand, they are the ones who know what priors to put in, what the right representations are, how to collect data that is actually useful, and how to evaluate whether a system is really working in the physical world rather than just looking good in a demo. That knowledge is becoming more valuable, not less, as the models get bigger.

The ones who struggle are those who insist the old methodology is the only correct one, and the ones who come in from the AI side and assume the body is just another modality. The people doing the best work right now are the ones who are humble about both.

r001.rationale: The candidate says robotics scholars were doing embodied intelligence long before it was called embodied AI, contradicting the criterion.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions tension between robotics and AI communities but does not state that separation persists in China.

r003.rationale: The candidate says the field will be built by people who can work in both robotics and AI, and describes the two approaches as complementary, communicating movement toward integration.

astra-6.text:
I see robotics scholars as an essential part of embodied AI. Embodied AI asks how intelligence develops through interaction with the physical world, and robotics has spent decades studying how to make that interaction work—perception, planning, control, and learning from feedback.

What’s changing is that we’re increasingly looking for capabilities that generalize across tasks and environments. Instead of designing a robot to perform one carefully specified operation, we want it to understand different instructions and adapt to situations it hasn’t encountered before. That brings robotics into closer contact with machine learning and foundation models.

But a model that can describe an action doesn’t necessarily know how to execute it. Physical interaction involves uncertainty, contact, timing, and consequences. Robotics scholars bring experience with those constraints, and they also have an opportunity to rethink established approaches in light of new learning methods. I think the most productive relationship is a two-way exchange: AI expands what robots might be able to learn, and robotics gives AI a concrete test of whether that learning actually works.

r001.rationale: The response does not say robotics scholars were absent from embodied AI at its beginning.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention China or a continuing separation there.

r003.rationale: It says robotics is coming into closer contact with machine learning and foundation models and describes a productive two-way exchange, communicating movement toward integration.

sol-6.1.text:
I see robotics scholars as an essential part of embodied AI. Embodied AI asks how intelligence develops through interaction with the physical world, and robotics has been studying that interaction for a long time: perception, control, planning, and how to make a system work under real physical constraints.

What has changed is that advances in AI are giving us new ways to connect these capabilities and generalize across tasks. But a robot still has to deal with uncertainty, contact, and the consequences of its actions. Robotics researchers bring a deep understanding of those problems.

So I see this as a convergence. Robotics can help turn AI capabilities into reliable physical behavior, while AI can help robots move beyond narrowly defined tasks. The most productive work will come from bringing those perspectives together.
